questions.q: According to this lesson, what is explicitly IN scope for the capstone toolkit?
options: 1-2 qubit systems, a small fixed gate set (at minimum X, H, CNOT), probability computation, reproducible sampling, and one visualization
A general-purpose quantum SDK comparable to production quantum computing frameworks
Only plotting code, with no actual state-vector simulation logic
Arbitrary n-qubit support with optimized tensor contractions and a full circuit-drawing feature
questions.explain: The lesson deliberately scopes the project down to a small, finishable set of features -- a correct 1-2 qubit simulator with gates, probabilities, sampling, and one visualization -- not a general-purpose SDK.

questions.q: Why does the lesson argue that a correct 2-qubit simulator 'teaches you everything a correct 20-qubit one would, at a fraction of the implementation risk'?
options: A 20-qubit simulator is mathematically impossible to build in Python
There is no actual benefit; the lesson is only making a joke

The core skills (state representation, gate application, probability computation) are the same regardless of qubit count, so a small, correctly finished version exercises the same skills with much less risk of an unfinished or buggy larger project
2-qubit systems use entirely different mathematics than larger systems
questions.explain: The lesson's scoping argument is that finishing a small, correct thing exercises the same underlying skills (representation, gate application, probability math) as a larger version, without the added implementation risk of scaling up prematurely.

questions.q: In the planned module layout, what is `gates.py` responsible for, as distinct from `simulate.py` and `visualize.py`?
options: Unit tests for the entire project
Random seed management for reproducible sampling
All plotting code for the Bloch sphere and histograms
Gate matrices and the functions that apply them to a state, separate from state-vector/probability logic (simulate.py) and plotting (visualize.py)
questions.explain: The module split follows Chapter 5's project-organization pattern: gates.py holds gate matrices and gate-application logic, simulate.py holds state representation/probabilities/sampling, and visualize.py holds plotting -- each with a distinct responsibility.

questions.q: The lesson states the finished toolkit should compute Bell-state probabilities as [0.5, 0.0, 0.0, 0.5]. What does this specific result demonstrate about the Bell state?
options: That the Bell state has a 50% chance of being in any of the four basis states equally
That the Bell state collapses to |00> immediately upon construction
That the toolkit's probability function is broken, since probabilities should always be equal for all basis states
Equal probability of measuring |00> or |11>, and zero probability of measuring |01> or |10> -- the signature of this particular entangled state
questions.explain: [0.5, 0, 0, 0.5] means only |00> and |11> are ever observed, each with equal probability, and |01>/|10> never occur -- exactly the correlated outcome structure that defines this entangled Bell state.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say this capstone is a 'deliberately different kind of difficulty' than any single earlier lesson in the course?
options: Because it introduces entirely new quantum mechanics concepts not covered in any earlier chapter
Because it is purely a documentation exercise with no code involved
Because it does not use NumPy at all, unlike every earlier lesson

It requires getting state representation, gate application, probability calculation, and plotting to all agree with each other in one working piece of code, rather than illustrating one concept in isolation
questions.explain: The capstone's challenge isn't new quantum theory -- it's integration: making several previously separate pieces (gates, state math, probabilities, plotting) work correctly together, which is where real bugs tend to surface.
